concepts.title: What is Living: Defining Properties of Life

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'What is Living: Defining Properties of Life' refers to.
questions.a: Living beings show defining properties such as growth, reproduction, metabolism, cellular organisation and consciousness, and the ability to respond to the environment, which distinguish them from non-living matter.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'What is Living: Defining Properties of Life'.
questions.a: Growth by increase in number of cells and self-consciousness are unique to organisms, while metabolism in toto is the surest defining feature of life.

concepts.title: Biodiversity: Number and Range of Species

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Biodiversity: Number and Range of Species' refers to.
questions.a: The earth holds enormous biodiversity, with roughly 1.7 to 1.8 million species described and named so far, ranging from microscopic bacteria to giant whales, and their number far exceeds what local experience suggests.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Biodiversity: Number and Range of Species'.
questions.a: Different regions differ in the number and range of species, which makes identification, nomenclature and classification essential before any biological study.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Biodiversity: Number and Range of Species' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.2 Diversity in the Living World (source: kebo101.txt section 1.2)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Nomenclature and Binomial Nomenclature' refers to.
questions.a: Scientific naming follows the binomial convention given by Carolus Linnaeus, where each organism gets a two-word name of generic and specific epithet written in italics with the generic name capitalised, guided by ICBN for plants and ICZN for animals.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Nomenclature and Binomial Nomenclature'.
questions.a: A single scientific name is universal, removing the confusion created by many local names for the same organism.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Nomenclature and Binomial Nomenclature' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Taxonomic Categories: Hierarchy of Classification' refers to.
questions.a: Classification arranges organisms in a taxonomic hierarchy of categories from species and genus through family, order, class, phylum to kingdom, where each higher category includes more general characters and more organisms.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Taxonomic Categories: Hierarchy of Classification'.
questions.a: Species is the lowest and basic taxonomic category, and the hierarchy moves from specific characters at the bottom to general characters at the top.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Taxonomic Categories: Hierarchy of Classification' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.3.1 Genus to Kingdom (source: kebo101.txt taxonomic categories sections)

concepts.title: Taxonomical Aids: Herbarium, Museum, Botanical Garden, Key

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Taxonomical Aids: Herbarium, Museum, Botanical Garden, Key' refers to.
questions.a: Taxonomical aids such as herbarium, botanical garden, museum, zoological park, key, flora, catalogue and monograph store and organise information about diversity, and a key uses paired contrasting statements called couplet and lead to identify organisms.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Taxonomical Aids: Herbarium, Museum, Botanical Garden, Key'.
questions.a: Keys, floras and monographs make identification possible even where specimens are absent, while herbaria and gardens preserve reference material.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Taxonomical Aids: Herbarium, Museum, Botanical Garden, Key' taught, and from which source text?
